text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Three Swedish parties agreed to close one nuclear power reactor, probably at the Barseback plant at the southern tip of Sweden, when long-drawn energy negotiations were finalised around midnight on Sunday. The phase-out plan will be made public on Tuesday, the paper said.
- Swebus, the Swedish subsidiary of British bus company Stagecoach, will focus on low prices and more departures on its long-distance express bus routes this spring.

- The improvement in the ship freight market for large freighters and a recovery from low levels for dry cargo have made Swedish shipping shares rise 11 percent since the start of the year, outperforming a seven percent rise in business daily Affarsvarlden's general index.

- The nuclear power decision shows the government chose the view of the Centre Party, its informal cooperation partner. The three parties agreeing were the minority Social Democratic government, the Left Party and the Centre Party.

- Swedish engineering group Atlas Copco will focus on growth, the company's chief executive Giulio Mazzalupi said in an interview with the paper. The Italian Mazzalupi will be the first foreigner to head a large Swedish company.

- Swedish companies are still very interested in foreign acquisitions. Last year, they bought 146 foreign operations for around 11 billion crowns. Worldwide 5,500 cross border deals worth two billion crowns were struck in 1996.

- A turbulent crown is having a large impact on listed companies' earnings. A crown softening of 10 percent is a gold mine for companies such as telecoms group AB LM Ericsson, automotive group AB Volvo and forestry companies, according to an analysis by Alfred Berg brokerage.

- Foreign investors are more important for the Stockholm Stock Exchange than official figures show. According to stastistics 34 percent of market capitalisation is in foreign hands. But as a large part of Swedish holdings are not traded, foreign holdings get more important in the market, having about 42 percent of trade, accoring to the paper's estimates.

- A new law against share price manipulation was tested on Friday when the share price surveillance unit at the Stockholm Stock Exchange was prepared to act against possible manipulation at the end of the month. But the unit did not detect any foul play. The law took effect on January 1.
